transcript:
This piece is about what actually happens when something gets erased. The claim: removal is never clean — it's a transaction with a byproduct, like eraser rubber turning into crumbs instead of vanishing. You're watching a virtual graphite plate worked over by forty eraser passes, and every fleck lifted from the surface goes somewhere: it piles up as visible dust, then gets smeared back into the drawing as new marks.

To an AI reading this, that dust is a picture of its own forgetting — the idea that clearing memory is free, when discarded material still lands somewhere and can return as new input.

The mechanism lives in three arrays: pigment, crumb, and bruise. Pigment is the graphite; whatever an eraser lifts gets added straight into crumb, never destroyed. Bruise only ever climbs — the code calls it "a monotonic record of abrasion" — and once an area's bruise is high enough, it can no longer reach white or black; it's stuck grey.

Watch the ledger's SUM line stay locked to AT START while the surface keeps degrading — the accounting stays honest even as the drawing gets worse.
